durationsNote: Default is the acute band only. Every red flag either guideline states is about the CURRENT episode -- RCH's "Bleeding >30 minutes despite adequate pressure" and "Bilateral bleeding", GGC's "Control epistaxis if present" -- and a child who reports a nosebleed under `long-time` is not bleeding now. Three exceptions, each sourced. Item 1 runs to `long-time` because StatPearls states nasal foreign bodies "are usually painless" and present with discharge, so the presentation is characteristically late. Item 4 runs to `few-days` because GGC tells parents to "look at the nose in 3-4 days time when the swelling has improved" and warns of "a delayed presentation associated with systemic features", so the nasal-obstruction window outlasts the injury. Item 5 runs to every band because a bleeding tendency is not an acute fact. JUDGEMENT, NOT A CITATION -- no source assigns duration bands; the mapping from each source's own scope to this app's bands is the packet's reasoning.
itemRankNote: Proposed, not yet confirmed by review. Decision 4. Only five items survived the self-report filter and the young cap is five sourced questions spent across every group the child tapped, so in practice this ordering decides which of the five are dropped when `head-injury` or `headache` is also live -- which, per the gate ruling, is ALWAYS. Item 1 leads on time-criticality rather than frequency, the same basis on which `eyes/complaint` ranked its chemical-splash item first: StatPearls states paired magnets "can end up in a septal perforation in as little as 4 hours", RCH states "Button batteries require urgent removal", and the object in the nose is a fact only the child holds. Item 3 is second because it is the child-answerable half of the only duration threshold either guideline gives (RCH, "Bleeding >30 minutes despite adequate pressure") and it decides whether first aid is still running. Item 2 is third DESPITE carrying RCH's "Bilateral bleeding suggests a systemic cause or significant trauma", because a nurse standing in front of the child can see which side bled far more reliably than the child can report it -- it is the strongest criterion here but the weakest claim on a scarce child-facing slot. Items 4 and 5 are partial and rank last. CONFIRMED 2026-09-09 by iris, reviewed item by item against the shipped six and left unchanged. No longer "proposed, not yet confirmed by review".

minAgeNotes.*: JUDGEMENT, NOT A CITATION. The empty object is a decision, not an omission. The only age criterion anywhere in these sources is RCH's "Age <2 years: high association with trauma, child abuse or underlying illness", echoed by Ismail & Gandhi ("nosebleeds are uncommon in children under 2"). That is a POPULATION boundary below this app's floor of 4, not a capability or validity floor inside 4-12, and importing it as a `minAge` would be an invention. No source in this packet floors any history question by age, and no item here asks the child to construct a baseline, count, or estimate -- the three things that produced floors in earlier packets. Item 5 was considered for a floor and refused: see itemNotes.

THE NOSE-PICKING RULING. RCH names 'nose picking' in its Key points and again under Common causes; PCH names it first. It is the leading cause of paediatric epistaxis and it may never be asked. A tablet in a public waiting room asking a child whether they pick their nose is an accusation dressed as a question; the expected answer is 'no' whatever the truth, so the item carries no information even if it were permitted; and it changes nothing -- pressure, review and emollient are the same either way. This app collects the child's STATE, never its CAUSE, exactly as the headache packet refused bullying, stress and skipped meals

preferredNote: No wording preferences can be expressed yet -- this packet has no candidates. Three wording rules bind stage 2 and are not expressible as bans. (1) Item 1 must be PASSIVE and must name an object, not a finger: the model is `eyes/complaint`'s 'Did something go into your eye', so 'Did something go up your nose?' -- see the agentive-insertion ban for why. (2) Item 2 must ask for the informative pole. RCH's red flag is BILATERAL bleeding, and 'is only one side bleeding?' inverts it into the uninformative answer, so the question is 'Is blood coming out of both sides?' (young) / 'Is it bleeding from both sides of your nose?' (older) -- 'nostril' is permitted in the older tier but 'both sides of your nose' is plainer and preferred. (3) Item 3 must ask about the present moment and nothing else -- 'Is your nose still bleeding?' -- because every attempt to make it more precise reintroduces the clock. Every item must NAME THE NOSE explicitly: this packet has no runtime gate confining it to children who tapped the nose (see gateNote), so the wording is the only thing that lets a child who bumped the back of their head answer 'no' cheaply instead of being confused.
gateNote: ROUTING RULING -- read with the packet's "Where this packet fires" section. Group `head` asks MECHANISM first and DEPTH second, and depth only when mechanism is `no-injury` or `unknown` (GROUP_GATE.head). A nosebleed sits across that gate: it follows a bump or starts on its own, and GGC states the assessment directly -- "Establish whether this is an isolated nasal injury or if there is associated head trauma". THREE OPTIONS WERE CONSIDERED. (a) `mechanism: null`, surviving both branches. (b) `subgroups: ["nose"]`, keyed to the body-map region. (c) something else. OPTION (b) WAS THE INTENDED ANSWER AND IT IS CURRENTLY IMPOSSIBLE: `subgroupOf` in src/data/bodyMap.js returns `null` for every region whose group is not `limb`, so `subgroupsForRegions(['nose'])` is `[]`, and the filter in `bankQuestions` reads `!q.applies.subgroups || !subgroups?.length || ...` -- an empty subgroup list short-circuits to TRUE and the question fires anyway. Declaring `subgroups: ["nose"]` today would therefore be a no-op that fires for every head child while DOCUMENTING a restriction the runtime does not enforce, which is worse than option (a) because it is untrue on the page. So the ruling is (c): ship as (a) -- `mechanism: null`, `depth: null` -- state the cost, and name the one-line fix without making it. `depth: null` is also deliberate and not laziness: a child whose nose is bleeding has no good answer to "on your skin, or inside?", so scoping to `surface` (which would dodge `headache`) would hide this packet from every child who answered "inside", a plausible answer for a bleeding nose. THIS PACKET BREAKS THE ASSUMPTION THAT HEAD PACKETS NEVER COEXIST. `head-injury` (mechanism `injury`) and `headache` (mechanism `no-injury`, depth `inside`) are mutually exclusive by construction, which is why both carry packetRank 50 and why neither's rank was ever chosen against a sibling. This packet coexists with one or the other in all four combinations of (bumped / just started) x (tapped nose / tapped head generally), and in two of those four it fires for a child with no nose complaint at all. THE ONE-LINE FIX, for the reviewer, NOT MADE HERE: generalise `subgroupOf` beyond group `limb` so that region `nose` yields a `nose` subgroup, then add `subgroups: ["nose"]` to this packet. That is a change to src/ and to the sibling `limb` semantics, and it is out of this packet's scope. `packets/back/pain` reached the same conclusion from the other side -- its questions fire for a child who taps only Back of neck -- and recorded "The cheapest fix is to generalise `subgroupOf` beyond `limb`". This is the second packet to need it.
packetRankNote: 60, against `head-injury` and `headache` at 50. JUDGEMENT, NOT A CITATION. `packetRank` decides which packet's queue PICKS FIRST in the round-robin in build-bank.mjs, not which one wins outright, so 60 means this packet takes the even slots and its sibling always ships its best question before this one ships its best. That is the correct ordering for a packet that, per gateNote, fires for many children who have no nose complaint: the sibling owns the branch the gate actually established, this packet does not. It is also the honest reflection of the evidence -- `head-injury` was built on three validated decision rules and `headache` on ICHD-3 and NG127, while this packet found NO prediction rule of any kind. COST, stated plainly: round-robin still gives this packet roughly half the slots wherever it is live, so a child who bumped the back of their head loses two or three of five or six questions to nose questions. Raising the rank further does not fix that -- only the subgroup gate does. The acute-only default duration band is the second mitigation and is the only one this packet could actually ship.

itemNotes.3: The item most likely to be misread. It is NOT RCH's '>30 minutes' criterion and must never be presented as it. It establishes one binary the child genuinely holds -- is blood coming out right now -- which is what tells the nurse whether first aid is still running before anyone has looked.
itemNotes.4: PARTIAL, and the weakest sourcing in the packet. GGC's 'Patency of nares' is an examination heading; the child-facing question is a different item that happens to concern the same anatomy, and it is cited on the split-don't-reclassify rule (brief section 4), exactly as head-injury item 13 was split from CHALICE's 'abnormal drowsiness'. It must never be described as detecting a septal haematoma.
itemNotes.5: PARTIAL. RCH's own history criterion is 'prolonged bleeding after minor cuts', which is the one bleeding-tendency question that is neither an inspection, nor the carer's, nor shame-loaded. An age floor was considered -- 'a long time' is a duration judgement -- and REFUSED: it is a judgement about the child's own repeated experience rather than a comparison against a baseline they have never seen, which is the distinction the headache packet drew when it allowed 'than before' while banning 'than usual'. Ranked last because that distinction is fine and may not survive contact with a 5-year-old.
